source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Breadth-limited BFS over model-proposed thoughts, with a model scoring each state and dropping weak ones, beats chain of thought on Game of 24 by a wide margin.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT breadth b=1 45%, b=5 74%. Best-of-100 CoT 49%.
quote: ToT with a breadth of b = 1 already achieves a success rate of 45%, while b = 5 achieves 74%.
limits: One benchmark of 100 puzzles; shallow tree (3 steps). Prompts hand-built per task.
agent_relevance: Keeping the best b states per step (breadth cap) is the pruning rule. Even b=1 (greedy with a state check) gave 45%, so much of the gain is checking states, not breadth.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Error analysis shows left-to-right chain of thought dies at the first step; the tree fixes it by checking early states.
numbers: About 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step (first three words, e.g. '4 + 9').
limits: Counted on Game of 24 only.
agent_relevance: Check at the first expansion, where most failures are born. Supports S6 pruning at shallow depth.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Cost: ToT at b=5 on Game of 24 uses about 5.5k completion tokens per case, close to 100 CoT trials, and still beats best-of-100.
numbers: Per case: IO best-of-100 $0.13 / 33%; CoT best-of-100 $0.47 / 49%; ToT $0.74 / 74%. Creative Writing ToT about 5x the tokens of CoT.
limits: GPT-4 prices of 2023. Gain per dollar differs by task. Table layout in the PDF text was garbled; cost-to-method mapping inferred from row order.
agent_relevance: Tree beats equal-cost sampling only when states can be checked. G7: count the cost.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Mini crosswords (depth up to 10, DFS with pruning on 'impossible' states): pruning by model judgment helps but is imperfect, and backtracking matters most.
numbers: ToT word-level success 60%, 4/20 games solved; oracle best state 7/20; no-pruning ablation worse overall but found 4/20 solutions, 3 of which pruned ToT could not; no-backtrack ablation 20% word level. IO and CoT under 16% word level.
quote: Given the state evaluation as a pruning heuristic is imperfect, we also explore ablating the pruning
limits: N=20 games. The model sometimes pruned a state that was actually correct because it did not know a rare word.
agent_relevance: A model-judged prune can cut the true path. Prune on cheap checks, keep pruned states in a revisit list. Backtracking is worth more than the pruning rule.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Generator is the bottleneck, not the evaluator, in Game of 24.
numbers: GPT-3.5 ToT 19% vs GPT-4 ToT 74%. GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%. GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%. Zero-shot ToT on GSM8K 90 vs CoT 86, StrategyQA 83 vs 82 (100 questions each).
limits: Small samples. On easy tasks the tree adds little for much cost.
agent_relevance: A cheap model can score states; spend the strong model on proposing. Do not grow a tree on tasks where one chain already works (G12).

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: MCTS where the same LLM acts as world model (predicts next state) and agent; reward mixes action likelihood, self-evaluation and state confidence.
numbers: Blocksworld, LLaMA-33B: RAP average 64% over 2/4/6-step problems, CoT near 0; 6-step problems solved 42% in 20 iterations (26% in 10). Reported 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT. Full Blocksworld (602 cases), Llama-2 70B, hard setting, RAP(10) 0.67 / 0.76 / 0.74 / 0.48 vs CoT 0.22 / 0.14 / 0.02 / 0.02 across plan lengths. GSM8K RAP 48.8% (+3% with aggregation).
limits: Reward terms are task dependent: action likelihood needed for plans, little help for math. Iteration count is the budget knob.
agent_relevance: Search budget is set in iterations, not depth. Hide history when scoring a step (saves iterations for early decisions).

source: Hao et al. (2023) RAP (introduction)
finding: Authors cite Huys et al. 2012 as the human basis for planning by simulating alternatives, but the LLM tree has no loss-driven pruning of the human kind; breadth is fixed by sampling.
numbers: Text cites Huys et al. 2012 in the opening on human planning; no human data tested.
limits: Citation link only; no test of human pruning.
agent_relevance: Human pruning (drop branches after a big loss) has not been copied by these systems; they prune by value score.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS over agent actions with an LLM value function, real environment feedback and self-reflection; beats ToT, RAP, Reflexion at the same trajectory count.
numbers: HumanEval GPT-4 pass@1 92.7 (base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0); GPT-3.5 83.8 vs ReAct 56.9, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1. WebShop score 75.9 (ReAct 53.8). HotpotQA GPT-3.5 EM 0.63 (ReAct 0.32, ToT 0.39, RAP 0.54). Game of 24 GPT-3.5 0.44 vs ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40.
limits: Needs the ability to revert to earlier states. Authors state higher compute cost than ReAct or Reflexion. Baselines run by the authors.
agent_relevance: Real feedback makes the tree useful. Without it the same paper's ablations drop.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) LATS (ablations and cost)
finding: Ablation on HotpotQA: every part matters; depth-first search is much worse than MCTS; LM value scoring is key.
numbers: LATS full 0.63; no LM heuristic 0.37; DFS 0.42; no reflection 0.58. At k=50: ToT 0.49 / 70.6 nodes, RAP 0.54 / 66.65 nodes, LATS 0.61 with fewer nodes on success. Best-of-250 ReAct 0.42, CoT-SC k=250 0.40.
limits: Node counts taken on success only.
agent_relevance: Value scoring plus reflection beat more sampling at equal calls (supports G3, G12).

source: Koh et al. (2024/2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first tree search in the real web environment with depth d, branching b and node budget c; performance grows with budget.
numbers: VisualWebArena GPT-4o: 18.9% to 26.4% (+39.7% relative). WebArena 19.2% (+28.0%). 200-task subset, depth 5, b 5: budget c=0 24.5%, c=5 32.0%, c=20 37.0% (+51%).
limits: Search limited to depth 5 and 5 actions per rollout for cost. Needs reversible state; real-site side effects are a risk.
agent_relevance: Direct S6 analogue: the three knobs d, b, c are the 'depth and pruning set by budget'. Gains rise with c up to 20, no plateau seen.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (depth, breadth, value function)
finding: Depth and breadth must grow together; value function quality sets the ceiling.
numbers: Table 3 (200 VWA tasks): d=1,b=3 26.0%; d=2,b=5 32.0%; d=3,b=3 31.5%; largest tree 37.0% (+51%). Value function: none 24.5, LLaVA 30.0, GPT-4o no self-consistency 28.5, SC n=5 32.5, SC n=20 37.0, ground-truth reward 43.5.
limits: Subset of 200 tasks; value function with 20 samples costs extra calls. Some depth/breadth cells ambiguous in PDF text.
agent_relevance: A noisy value model caps pruning quality. Spend samples on the value check, not only on proposals.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (versus sampling, by difficulty)
finding: Search beats sampling more trajectories at equal compute, and the gain peaks at medium difficulty, where depth 5 fits.
numbers: Re-ranking n runs plateaus near 7 runs at 30% vs search c=20 37.0%. By difficulty: easy 34.2 to 42.3 (+24%), medium 12.7 to 22.2 (+75%), hard 10.2 to 14.9 (+47%).
limits: Authors suggest hard tasks need deeper trees; untested here.
agent_relevance: Matches G12: search pays where a foothold exists. Set depth by expected task length.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench
finding: Plain LLMs cannot do search-style planning on classical domains; tasks needing real lookahead are worst.
numbers: Blocksworld plan generation: GPT-4 206/600 (34.3%), Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%). Mystery Blocksworld (renamed objects) GPT-4 26/600 (4.3%). Plan verification about 32-48%; replanning 76.8%.
limits: Zero/one-shot, temperature 0, 2023 models. Table rows partly garbled in PDF text.
agent_relevance: Baseline showing why search is added; the drop under renaming suggests pattern recall, not search.

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs?
finding: A reasoning model (o1) with internal search jumps on small Blocksworld but not on obfuscated or long problems, and costs far more.
numbers: o1-preview zero-shot Blocksworld 587/600 (97.8%), o1-mini 56.6%; Mystery 52.8%; Randomized Mystery 37.3%. Problems needing 20-40 steps: 23.63% (110 instances). Fast Downward 100% in 0.265 s vs o1 about 40-111 s. Cost per 100 instances: GPT-4o-mini $0.02 vs o1-preview $42.12.
limits: Preliminary; o1 internals hidden; no correctness guarantee. Unsolvable-instance detection poor (16% correct on randomized mystery).
agent_relevance: Internal search scales poorly in depth, as depth-limited planning predicts. A classical solver beats it on cost and certainty, so call code when possible (G5).

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through the Lens of Efficiency
finding: Instead of calling the LLM at every node, ask it once to write the successor function and goal test as code, then run ordinary BFS or DFS. Sound, complete, and nearly free.
numbers: Game of 24: all 1362 instances handled correctly (1361 solvable, 1 unsolvable flagged) in 1.92 to 6.83 s total; ToT reported 74-75% on 100 problems with many LLM calls each. Crosswords: 20/20 solved, 5.5 to 346 s total. BlocksWorld 502/502 in 0.56 to 9.7 s. About 1.2 LLM interactions to write the successor function. PrOntoQA 4000/4000.
limits: Needs a problem whose rules can be stated as code. Crossword test assumed 10 candidate answers per clue.
agent_relevance: Strongest result for S6: put the tree in code, use the model to write the move generator and checker, not to walk the tree. Matches G5 and G3.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search (complexity audit)
finding: Complexity audit: LLM tree methods lose soundness and completeness and gain no efficiency from that loss.
numbers: Estimated LLM calls on the 24 game (1362 tasks): CoT/ReAct 1362, RAP 4086, ToT 245K, GoT 102K, LATS 68K; their method needs only a few LLM calls (search runs in code).
limits: Estimates are the authors' formulas, not measured bills; table columns partly garbled in PDF text.
agent_relevance: Count LLM calls per node when sizing the tree. Budget in model calls, not nodes.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws: Compute-Optimal Inference for LLM Problem-Solving
finding: A reward-balanced tree (REBASE) that spends expansion budget by node reward beats both sampling and MCTS at equal FLOPs; a small model plus tree can beat a bigger model.
numbers: Llemma-7B with REBASE matches Llemma-34B at about 2x fewer FLOPs on MATH500 and GSM8K; REBASE with 7B beats 34B plain majority voting at all budgets; fitted log10(C)=1.19 log10(N)+2.03 for optimal model size.
limits: Math only, Llemma family, trained process reward model.
agent_relevance: Pruning by reward-proportional width is cheaper than MCTS rollouts. A soft budget split is a working alternative to hard pruning.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Chopping Trees: Semantic Similarity Based Dynamic Pruning for Tree-of-Thought (SSDP)
finding: Merge sibling branches whose text embeddings are near-identical, keep one representative.
numbers: Up to 2.3x speedup vs tree-search baselines, accuracy within about 5% of the best baseline, 85-90% fewer nodes explored. Qwen2.5-1.5B nodes explored per sample: MATH500 11.5 vs 53.3, GSM8K 4.8 vs 19.5.
limits: Small models, NeurIPS workshop paper, GSM8K and MATH500 only, accuracy loss up to 5%.
agent_relevance: Many branches are copies; collapsing duplicates by code is a safe prune. Fits G4: samples from one model are not independent.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search (UAA)
finding: Siblings sampled from one state are mostly duplicates; the spread among siblings predicts how much to expand, so set per-step width from it.
numbers: Most continuations have similarity above 0.95. UAA cuts tokens up to 90% and latency up to 9x at comparable accuracy; Llama3.1-8B GSM8K tokens 8.22k to 5.43k and time 114.75 s to 74.58 s; GPT-4o with PRM variance about 40% fewer tokens; StrategyQA Qwen3-32B beam 64.33% to 72.00% with 2.02k to 1.64k tokens. MCTS settings: width 4, max depth 40, 100 iterations.
limits: Best estimator needs hidden-state embeddings; closed models use score variance, tested only on GPT-4o; theory assumes Lipschitz and persistence.
agent_relevance: Cheap rule for S6: when siblings agree, shrink width; when they diverge, widen. Depth/width by uncertainty, not a fixed budget.

source: Li et al. (2026) Spend Less, Reason Better: Budget-Aware Value Tree Search (BAVT)
finding: Remaining-budget ratio is used as an exponent on node values, so search moves from wide to greedy as the budget runs out; a residual critic scores progress, not state quality.
numbers: Four multi-hop QA sets, OSS-20B: BAVT at 5 tool calls averages 0.338 EM vs baseline 0.334 at 20 calls (baseline at 5 calls 0.194). Qwen3-30B instruct baseline flat: 0.289 (low) to 0.293 (high) EM. Tiers: 5/10/20 tool calls.
limits: Baseline is parallel sampling with voting; critic costs tokens; search calls dominate dollar cost; no human data.
agent_relevance: Clearest budget-to-pruning rule: shrink breadth as spend rises. Good G12 evidence that management beats more compute.

source: Fang et al. (2026) SCULPT: Constraint-Guided Pruned MCTS for Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Prune actions by symbolic checks (units, types, magnitude, depth) inside MCTS over agent workflows.
numbers: Pruned 34.2% of branches on average (15 rounds, 3 datasets, std 3.1%). 28% less optimisation time, 31% lower API cost. GPT-4o-mini executor: GSM8K 93.8, MATH 57.2 vs AFlow 93.5 / 56.2. GPT-5.2 executor: MATH 89.9 vs IO 81.8, GSM8K 97.8 vs IO 96.3 but 24,142 vs 1,120 tokens.
limits: Gain over strongest baseline only +1 to +2 points; GSM8K near ceiling; math only; magnitude checks need execution traces.
agent_relevance: Code-side checks prune safely; but gain over plain IO at 20x tokens is small on easy sets (G7).

source: Luo et al. (2026) TabTracer: Monte Carlo Tree Search for Complex Table Reasoning
finding: MCTS with typed operations, step checks, state hashing, deduplication and budget-aware pruning; rollback to saved snapshots.
numbers: Up to 6.7% accuracy gain over best baselines; tokens cut 59-84%. Removing SelectColumns drops CRT accuracy from 70.5% to 52-53%; removing FilterRows costs 2-4 points and about 600 more tokens. Large tables WikiTQ 73-79% vs Table-Critic 64-68%.
limits: Table QA only; ablations on CRT (728 items).
agent_relevance: Reversible state with snapshots makes backtracking cheap. Hashing states prunes repeats at zero model cost.

source: Long (2023) Large Language Model Guided Tree-of-Thought
finding: A rule-based checker flags dead-end Sudoku boards and a controller backtracks; the LLM only proposes fills.
numbers: 10 puzzles per size: ToT solved 10/10 of 3x3, 9/10 of 4x4, 8/10 of 5x5 (max 100 conversation rounds); one-shot and few-shot near 0.5 on larger boards.
limits: Tiny sample (10 per size), rule-based controller, no cost report.
agent_relevance: A code check of partial state decides the prune; the LLM never judges validity. Same lesson as G3 and G5.

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search: Learning to Search in Language
finding: Training a model on text traces that include dead ends and backtracking beats training on only optimal paths.
numbers: Countdown: SoS model 51.27% on held-out inputs vs 25.73% for the optimal-path model (+25 points); finetuning with STaR/APA solves 36% of previously unsolved problems and about 4% of problems no heuristic solver solved. 57.1% of 285,501 training trajectories were correct.
limits: Trained from scratch on one game; not a prompting result.
agent_relevance: Shows exposure to failed branches matters, but our agent cannot train. At most, show dead-end examples in context.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Best test-time search method depends on problem difficulty: search against a process reward model helps on harder items, plain sampling on easier ones.
numbers: Not opened this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; claim recalled, not read here. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Supports G12.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Humans prune a decision tree at a branch after a large loss and keep it cut even when the best path lies behind it. This is the human paradigm that the LLM tree systems above do not copy.
numbers: Not opened this session (human numbers belong to the other angle files).
limits: Cited as the human anchor only. No LLM replication of loss-driven pruning was found in the papers read.
agent_relevance: Open test for the agent: does a branch with an early loss get dropped though it leads to the best result? Log it.

source: Gap note across sources read (2023-2026)
finding: No paper read here tests an LLM on the human pruning paradigm (loss-driven pruning, limited-depth planning) or compares LLM search depth with human depth.
numbers: 0 of 15 opened papers report a human-versus-LLM depth or pruning comparison. Web search quota was exhausted and the arXiv and OpenAlex listing APIs rate-limited, so a targeted search could not be run.
limits: Absence of finding, not proof of absence. Repeat the search once quota refills.
agent_relevance: Treat human-to-LLM pruning claims as unsupported until found.
